title: The small team inside the office
allegory: A circuit is like the small team inside a huge office that actually handles one job: everyone writes on one shared whiteboard, but only a few desks, passing notes that change where the next desk looks, get this particular answer out.
map: GPT-2 small's 144 attention heads (plus its MLPs)
the shared whiteboard everyone reads and writes
the small team that handles 'who gets the drink'
the IOI circuit: 26 heads in 7 classes
one desk's note changing where another desk looks
composition: a later head's Q, K or V reading what an earlier head wrote
proving the team alone can do it, nobody's missing, nobody's idle

cap.1: 'When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to…' GPT-2 says 'Mary'. Somewhere in its 144 attention heads, something worked out who. Which ones?
cap.2: A circuit is the small subgraph of heads and MLPs that together produce one behaviour. For this sentence pattern, indirect object identification, Wang et al. went looking for it in GPT-2 small.
cap.3: Circuit hypothesis: a sparse subgraph of components and the residual-stream edges between them that accounts for a task metric, here logit[IO] − logit[S] at the final position.

cap.1: Picture a huge office where everyone writes on one shared whiteboard. For this job only a small team matters: a spotter, a messenger and an announcer.
cap.2: Every head reads from and writes to the residual stream, so any head can influence any later one. A circuit is the handful whose reads and writes actually carry this behaviour.
cap.3: Heads communicate only through the residual stream: a later head's Q, K or V reads a subspace an earlier head wrote (Q-, K-, V-composition). A circuit names which compositions matter.

cap.1: The spotter notices 'John' appeared twice. The messenger carries 'ignore John' to the end. The announcer reads the names, skips John, and says 'Mary'.
cap.2: Duplicate-token and induction heads flag the repeated name. S-inhibition heads (7.3, 7.9, 8.6, 8.10) move that flag to the last position. Name movers (9.6, 9.9, 10.0) attend to the other name and copy it.
cap.3: S-inhibition heads V-compose the duplicate flag from S2 to END; it enters the name movers through their queries (Q-composition), suppressing attention to S so their OV circuits copy IO.

chapters.name: Three tests
chapters.title: what counts as finding a circuit
values: the team alone does the job?

cap.1: Seeing who talks to whom isn't proof. You must show the team alone can do the job, nobody important is missing, and nobody on it is idle.
cap.2: Wang et al. judged their 26-head, 7-class circuit by faithfulness (it alone reproduces the behaviour), completeness (nothing important outside it) and minimality (nothing inside is redundant).
cap.3: These criteria, tested by causal intervention (patching, ablation) rather than attention plots, are the part that outlasted the specific circuit. They apply to any claimed mechanism.

cap.1: Real teams are messy. One desk shouts the wrong name. Remove an announcer and an understudy takes over, so knocking out one head can look harmless.
cap.2: Negative name movers (10.7, 11.10) write against the right answer; 10.7 alone makes the wrong name about 7x more likely. Backup name movers step in when the main ones are ablated.
cap.3: Backup heads repair ablations, so single-component ablation systematically understates importance. A circuit is components pulling against each other to a net result, not a tidy machine.

chapters.name: Heads or features?
chapters.verdict: Either unit, same standard: faithful, complete, minimal.

cap.1: How to carve up the team is still debated: teams of whole heads (the classic) or of finer 'features' (newer). Either way, you prove it the same way.
cap.2: Current method: circuits of heads and MLPs found with patching, as in IOI. Emerging: circuits of sparse features, since MLP neurons are polysemantic (transcoders, attribution graphs in [1.4.2]). You need: patching plus the three tests.
cap.3: Head-level circuits like IOI are established; feature-level circuits via transcoders and attribution graphs are the active frontier, with error nodes marking what they miss. The validation logic transfers unchanged.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Where you would steer or fix a behaviour

cap.1: Finding the team turns 'the model can do X' into 'these parts do X, like this'. That is what understanding means, and it shows you where to steer.
cap.2: The loop repeats all course: guess a mechanism, find candidates cheaply (attention patterns, DLA), then test with patching. Induction heads and IOI are your two worked circuits.
cap.3: Circuits give causal, component-level explanations: the basis for targeted interventions, and for checking whether a steering or safety method acts where you think it does.

coda.title: Knock out parts of the team (toy numbers)

readouts.label: naive guess: 2.8 minus what the removed parts normally add
what happened
readouts.f: (nm && !bk) ? 'backups stepped in: the drop understates what the name movers do' : (neg && !nm ? 'removing the hecklers raised the score' : 'matches the naive guess')

caption.1: Toy numbers. Knock out the announcers: the score drops far less than you'd expect, because understudies step in. Knock out the heckler and the score goes up.
caption.2: Ablating the name movers alone lets backups take over, so the drop understates their role. Ablate the backups too and the full effect shows. Removing negative movers raises the logit difference.
caption.3: Illustrative values, not IOI measurements. Self-repair makes single-component ablation understate importance; joint ablations and path patching are how you see past it.

hamming.what: A small set of heads and MLPs, and the connections between them, that together carry out one identifiable behaviour.
hamming.when: When you want to explain how a model does a specific task, not just that it can.
hamming.why: It turns a capability into a mechanism with an address that you can test, and eventually edit or steer.

object.title: The relay board
object.subtitle: A wiring board with only the team that matters connected: tokens in, answer out.

cap.1: The relay board: tokens on the left, the answer on the right, and only the team that matters wired in between.
cap.2: Nodes are head classes from the IOI circuit; wires are the compositions between them through the residual stream.
cap.3: A circuit diagram is a hypothesis about which edges of the full computational graph carry the task metric.

cap.1: Follow the wires: the repeated 'John' lights the spotters, whose flag the messengers carry toward the announcers.
cap.2: Duplicate-token heads flag S2 as a repeat; S-inhibition heads move that flag to the final position.
cap.3: Duplicate-token heads write a 'duplicated' signal; S-inhibition heads V-compose it from S2 to END.

cap.1: The announcers look at both names, but the messengers' note steers them away from 'John'. So they copy 'Mary'.
cap.2: The inhibition signal enters the name movers' queries, changing where they look, not what they copy.
cap.3: Q-composition from S-inhibition heads suppresses attention to S; the name movers' OV circuits copy IO to the logits.

cap.1: The dark node pulls the other way, pushing 'John' up. The pale node sits idle, waiting to take over if the announcers are removed.
cap.2: Negative name movers write against the answer; backup name movers only act once the main ones are ablated.
cap.3: Components with opposing contributions and self-repair make circuits messier than a clean relay, and ablations harder to read.

cap.1: 26 heads out of 144, in seven roles. The board is a claim you test by cutting wires, not a picture you admire.
cap.2: Wang et al. validated it with faithfulness, completeness and minimality, measured by intervention.
cap.3: Patching into specific edges (path patching) is what licenses drawing each wire on this board.

predict.q: You zero-ablate the main name movers and the IOI score drops only a little. Do they not matter?

options.t: They matter: backup heads stepped in, so ablation understates them
They don't matter much: small drop, small role

predict.why: Backup name movers take over when the main ones are removed, so single-head ablation understates importance.

predict.q: Where does the 'ignore John' signal enter the name mover heads?

options.t: Their queries: it changes where they look
Their values: it changes what they copy
It skips them and goes straight to the logits

predict.why: Path patching into the name movers' queries lights up the S-inhibition heads; keys and values show much less.

predict.q: Which of these is NOT one of Wang et al.'s circuit criteria?
predict.why: The criteria are faithfulness, completeness and minimality, each tested by intervention. Clean plots prove nothing.

object.where: Any claim that a few parts of a big system do one job: a mechanism with an address, tested by cutting wires.
